questions.q: In the Monty Hall problem, why does switching win with probability 2/3 rather than 1/2?
options: The host opens a door uniformly at random, so switching has no information value
The host is constrained to always reveal a goat among the two unpicked doors, so his reveal carries information about where the car is
There are three doors, so every strategy wins with probability 1/3 regardless of switching
Switching only helps if the host opens the door you originally picked
questions.explain: Because the host always reveals a goat from the doors you didn't pick, switching wins exactly when your original pick was a goat (probability 2/3), not when it was the car (probability 1/3).

questions.q: In Bertrand's box paradox, why is P(other coin is gold | drawn coin is gold) equal to 2/3 rather than 1/2?
options: Because the GG box is twice as likely to produce a gold coin on the draw as the GS box, so gold draws are not split evenly between them
Because silver coins are heavier and more likely to be drawn first
Because there are three boxes, so every conditional probability must be a multiple of 1/3
Because the paradox has no well-defined answer
questions.explain: GG offers two ways to draw gold while GS offers only one, so among draws that come up gold, GG is twice as represented as GS, giving P(other gold | gold drawn) = 2/3.

questions.q: For a two-child family, what is P(both children are boys | at least one child is a boy)?
questions.explain: Of the four equally likely birth orders (BB, BG, GB, GG), 'at least one boy' rules out only GG, leaving BB, BG, GB — one of three equally likely outcomes is BB.

questions.q: Why does P(both boys | the older child is a boy) differ from P(both boys | at least one child is a boy)?
options: Specifying the older child is a boy is a stronger, asymmetric statement that rules out GB in addition to GG, leaving only BB and BG
Birth order has no effect on probability in this problem
The second statement is logically impossible to condition on
questions.explain: 'At least one boy' leaves three equally likely orders (BB, BG, GB); 'the older is a boy' leaves only two (BB, BG), so the conditional probability of both boys rises from 1/3 to 1/2.

questions.q: What is the common mechanism behind all three brainteasers in this lesson (Monty Hall, Bertrand's box, boy-or-girl)?
options: Each has a genuinely undefined probability with no correct answer
In each case, the conditioning event is more likely under one hypothesis than another, so a flat 50/50 split of remaining hypotheses is wrong — Bayes' theorem on the true sample space is required
All three require calculus to resolve
All three are resolved by assuming independence between the conditioning event and the quantity of interest
questions.explain: In each puzzle, naive intuition assumes the conditioning event splits evenly across remaining hypotheses; in fact it favors some outcomes over others, so correctly enumerating the sample space or applying Bayes' theorem is required to get the right answer.
